Example Widgets Inc. Opens a Solar-Powered Widget Plant

By Jordan Sample

March 14, 2026

Example Widgets Inc. opened its first solar-powered widget plant on Tuesday, a sprawling single-story building that the company says will produce four million widgets a year without drawing power from the regional grid. The plant sits on a former parking lot at the edge of Sampletown, and its roof is covered from edge to edge with photovoltaic panels that feed a bank of batteries in the basement.

Company engineers spent two years redesigning the widget press so that it could run on direct current. The old presses used large alternating-current motors that were cheap to buy but wasted a surprising amount of energy as heat. The new presses use smaller motors and a flywheel that stores energy between strokes, which the company says cuts electricity use per widget by almost forty percent.

"We wanted to prove that a factory does not have to be loud, hot and hungry for power," said the plant manager, Riley Placeholder, during a tour for reporters. "Most of what you hear in here now is the ventilation fans and the click of the sorting arms." Visitors on the tour were asked to wear ear protection only near the packaging line.

How the batteries work

The battery bank is made of recycled cells taken from retired delivery vans. Each cell is tested and graded before it is placed on a rack, and cells that fall below a set capacity are sent back for recycling. The company says the bank can run the plant through a cloudy day and most of a night, and that the plant will draw from the grid only in long stretches of bad weather.

Measure Old plant New plant
Energy per widget 1.0 unit 0.6 units
Widgets per year 3 million 4 million

Analysts who follow the widget industry said the plant was a useful test but warned that its costs would take years to recover. Solar panels and batteries are cheaper than they were a decade ago, they noted, but a plant that must store a full day of power still needs far more batteries than one that can lean on the grid at night.

The company plans to publish a full year of energy data from the plant next spring. If the numbers hold up, it says, two older plants will be converted using the same design, starting with the one in Exampleville.
